question: Is it okay to hate your relatives?
summary: Luke 14:26 has Jesus state baldly that no one can be his disciple without hating father, mother, wife, children, brothers, sisters, and his own life. Ephesians, by contrast, commands honoring father and mother as the first commandment with promise (6:2), commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church (5:25), and observes that no one ever hated his own flesh (5:29). The discipleship hatred Jesus demands is exactly what the Pauline household codes forbid.

reconcile.connective: GILL argues Jesus never enjoins literal hatred — contrary to God's own law — but only that family not be loved more than Christ.

discrepancy.connective: Gerd Theissen argues Luke's family-renunciation ethic reflects the real practice of the wandering-charismatic Jesus movement — a stance the later household code genuinely reverses.

skeptic.name: Gerd Theissen
skeptic.attribution: Gerd Theissen, Sociology of Early Palestinian Christianity, trans. John Bowden (Philadelphia: Fortress, 1978), pp. 8-16

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley devotes a page-286 parallel-column heading, 'Kindred, how regarded: Hated. — Loved.', setting Luke 14:26 directly against Ephesians 5:25, 33, and resolves it via the Hebrew-idiom sense of 'hate' as 'to love less,' quoting Moses Stuart and Henry Alford.

link.title: GotQuestions: What did Jesus mean when He instructed us to hate our father and mother (Luke 14:26)?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment of the same comparative-hatred reading (cross-referencing Mark 7:9-13 and 1 Timothy 5:8 rather than Ephesians, but directly on-topic to Luke 14:26 itself).

excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: not that proper hatred of any, or all of these, is enjoined by Christ; for this would be contrary to the laws of God, to the first principles of nature, to all humanity, to the light of nature, to reason and divine revelation: but that these are not to be preferred to Christ, or loved more than he …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly denies that Jesus commands literal hatred, grounding the denial in 'the laws of God' — the same divine-law footing Ephesians' household commands stand on — and reduces 'hate' to not-preferring-above-Christ, which is compatible with honoring parents and loving one's wife.
excerpts.source_note_text:
If any man come to me,.... Not in a corporeal, but in a spiritual way; nor barely to hear him preach; but so come, as that he believes in him, applies to him for grace, pardon, righteousness, life, and salvation; professes to be his, submits to his ordinances, and desires to be a disciple of his;
and hate not his father and mother, and wife and children, and brethren and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple: not that proper hatred of any, or all of these, is enjoined by Christ; for this would be contrary to the laws of God, to the first principles of nature, to all humanity, to the light of nature, to reason and divine revelation: but that these are not to be preferred to Christ, or loved more than he, as it is explained in Mat 10:37 yea, these are to be neglected and forsaken, and turned from with indignation and resentment, when they stand in the way of the honour and interest of Christ, and dissuade from his service: such who would be accounted the disciples of Christ, should be ready to part with their dearest relations and friends, with the greatest enjoyment of life, and with life itself, when Christ calls for it; or otherwise they are not worthy to be called his disciples. The Ethiopic version inserts, "his house", into the account.
